tip: Avoir beau + verb has nothing to do with beauty: 'on a beau chercher' means 'no matter how hard we search'. It sets up wasted effort, then the letdown.
'Leur' here means 'to them', not just 'them': 'nous leur avons laissé' = we left a message TO them. It's the give-to pronoun, distinct from 'les' (them as direct object).
'Vînt' looks like a typo but it's the imperfect subjunctive, a literary tense. In everyday speech you'd just say 'qu'elle vienne me voir'.
The 'ne' in 'avant que le soleil ne se couchât' isn't a negation – it's a decorative 'ne' that 'avant que' attracts. The sun still sets.
One word or two flips the meaning: 'quoique' (one word, as here) = 'although'; 'quoi que' (two words) = 'whatever'. Quoique la nuit fût sombre = although the night was dark.
After 'le seul ... qui', French switches to the subjunctive: 'le seul homme qui eût du courage'. The claim reads as a judgement, not plain fact.
French uses faire for the state of the sky: 'il fait nuit' means 'it's dark', literally 'it makes night'. That's why the verb here shows up as 'fît'.
'Mettre du sien' means to pull your weight, literally 'to put some of one's own'. 'Chacun y mette du sien' = everyone pitches in.
